questions.q: ShopFlow grows in three stages. Which one do you build first, and why?
questions.explain: Start simple. In stage 3 the single checkout transaction becomes a saga across services, which is the price of microservices. You pay it only when there is a real reason.
options: Services, because they scale best from day one
A monolith with clean modules, because one process and one database keep checkout a single transaction
A modular monolith with one database server per module
A saga across four services

questions.q: In stage 1, users, catalog and orders share the database connection, cache, event bus and queue. What else do they share?
questions.explain: Modules share infrastructure and nothing else. Orders never reads the catalog's code; things that should happen after a sale listen for an order.placed event.
options: Their private helper functions
Nothing: each module is created by one function that is its public API
Their tables, which any module may update
One big utils.ts file with all the business rules

questions.q: Why does ShopFlow store prices as whole cents in an INT column?
questions.explain: Whole cents add up exactly. You divide by 100 only when you show a price.
options: Integers use less disk space than text
Floating-point numbers cannot store most decimals exactly, so sums like 0.1 + 0.2 go slightly wrong
PostgreSQL has no decimal types
So prices can never be changed

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: 0.1 + 0.2 is 0.30000000000000004. Cents are whole numbers, so they add exactly. Two mugs at 1200 cents cost 2400 cents, shown as 24.00.
options:
false
true
24.00

true
true
24.00

false
true
24

false
false
24.00

questions.q: The products table has CHECK (stock >= 0). What is it for, if the checkout code already checks the stock?
questions.explain: Defence in depth. The database refuses the write with an error, so a bug cannot silently sell stock that does not exist.
options: It makes queries faster
It is the last line of defence: if a bug ever gets past the code, the database itself refuses negative stock
It replaces the need for transactions
It sets the stock to 0 when it would go negative

questions.q: Why does the sessions table store only a hash of the session token?
questions.explain: The token goes to the client once. On each request the server hashes the token it receives and looks up the hash, together with an expiry date.
options: Hashes are shorter, so the table is smaller
If the database leaks, the hashes cannot be used to log in, because the real tokens are not in it
So the server can show the token to the user again later
Because PostgreSQL cannot store random strings

questions.q: Ada registers with { "email": …, "password": …, "role": "admin" }. What does ShopFlow do with role?
questions.explain: If the body could set role, anyone could make themselves an admin. The role comes from the database, never from the request. Her later attempt to create a product got 403.
options: Saves it, because the user asked for it
Saves it only if the password is long enough
Ignores it: every new account is a customer; admins are promoted by a setup script on the server
Answers 500 because the field is unknown

questions.q: The Credentials schema parses a registration body. What does this print?
questions.explain: The e-mail is trimmed and lower-cased, so Ada@Example.com and ada@example.com are one account. The object schema keeps only the fields it knows, so role never reaches the insert.
options: { email: 'ada@example.com', password: 's3cret-pass' }
{ email: 'Ada@Example.com', password: 's3cret-pass', role: 'admin' }
{ email: 'ada@example.com', password: 's3cret-pass', role: 'admin' }
{ email: '  Ada@Example.com ', password: 's3cret-pass' }

questions.q: Why does login give the same answer, Wrong e-mail or password, for an unknown e-mail and for a wrong password?
questions.explain: Different answers would let anyone test a list of e-mails. For the same reason the code verifies a decoy hash when the e-mail is unknown, so both cases also take the same time.
options: To keep the code shorter
So an attacker cannot find out which e-mail addresses have accounts
Because the database cannot tell the two cases apart
So users try again more often

questions.q: When the e-mail is unknown, login still runs verifyPassword against a decoyHash. Why?
questions.explain: Password hashing is slow on purpose. Skipping it for unknown e-mails would make those answers measurably faster, a timing leak.
options: To create the account automatically
So "no such e-mail" takes as long as "wrong password"; otherwise the response time would reveal which e-mails exist
To slow down the server on purpose for every user
Because verifyPassword must be called exactly once per request

questions.q: The catalog module does not check permissions. Where does ShopFlow check them?
questions.explain: The module does not know who is calling. The HTTP route authenticates the user from the bearer token, calls authorize(user, "product:create"), and only then calls the module.
options: Nowhere: products are public
At the edge, in the HTTP layer, where the logged-in user is known
In the database, with a trigger
In the browser, before the request is sent

questions.q: These are ShopFlow's roles. What does this print?
questions.explain: A customer may create orders but not products. The admin's *:* matches every permission. The HTTP layer turns a false into a 403 AuthorizationError.
options: true false true
true true true
false false true
true false false

questions.q: Which statement takes stock safely, so two customers can never both buy the last mug?
questions.explain: The check and the change are one statement. PostgreSQL locks the row for the first UPDATE, and the second one sees the new stock. If there is not enough, no row matches and RETURNING returns nothing.
options: SELECT stock, then in JavaScript if (stock >= qty) run UPDATE products SET stock = $new
UPDATE products SET stock = stock - $1 WHERE sku = $2 AND stock >= $1 RETURNING id, price_cents
UPDATE products SET stock = stock - $1 WHERE sku = $2, and fix negative stock later
DELETE FROM products WHERE stock = 0 before each checkout

questions.q: A teammate replaced the conditional UPDATE with "read, then write". Two checkouts for the last mug run at the same time. What does this print?
questions.explain: Both read 1 before either writes, so both decide there is enough. Both write 0: two mugs sold, one existed. This gap between reading and writing is a race condition; the single conditional UPDATE has no gap.
options: [ 'ada: bought', 'linus: bought' ] left: 0
[ 'ada: bought', 'linus: sold out' ] left: 0
[ 'ada: bought', 'linus: bought' ] left: -1
[ 'ada: sold out', 'linus: sold out' ] left: 1

questions.q: Now the check and the change happen in one step, like the conditional UPDATE. What does this print?
questions.explain: With no await between the check and the change, nothing can run in between. The second checkout sees 0 and gets "sold out", just as the second UPDATE sees the new stock in PostgreSQL.
options: [ 'ada: bought', 'linus: sold out' ] left: 0
[ 'ada: bought', 'linus: bought' ] left: 0
[ 'ada: bought', 'linus: bought' ] left: -1
[ 'ada: sold out', 'linus: bought' ] left: 0

questions.q: A client sends { "sku": "mug", "quantity": 1, "priceCents": 1 } to /checkout. Which price does ShopFlow charge?
questions.explain: The price comes from the database, never from the request, so a client cannot choose its own price. The checkout schema does not even read priceCents.
options: 1 cent, the price in the request
The price from the database, returned by the UPDATE … RETURNING price_cents
The average of both prices
It answers 500 because the field is unknown

questions.q: Ada checks out a T-shirt and a mug. The T-shirt line succeeds, then the mug has no stock. What happens to the T-shirt's stock?
questions.explain: All lines, the order, its lines and the audit event run in one transaction. The final product list in the lesson still shows 5 T-shirts after the 409.
options: It stays taken, and Ada gets half an order
It is put back: the ConflictError rolls back the whole transaction, so the order is all or nothing
It is put back the next night by a scheduled job
The T-shirt is shipped and the mug is back-ordered

questions.q: Why is order.placed published after db.transaction returns, not inside it?
questions.explain: Side effects happen after the commit. A crash between the commit and the publish could still lose the event, which the outbox milestone fixes.
options: Events cannot be published from async functions
So no listener ever reacts to an order that is later rolled back, such as sending a receipt for it
Because publishing inside a transaction is slower
So the event includes the database password

questions.q: This fake transaction throws halfway. What does this print?
questions.explain: The event is published only after the transaction finished without an error. Order 2 failed, so no receipt goes out for an order that does not exist.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: 401 means "we do not know who you are", 403 means "we know you, and you may not do this", 409 means "this conflicts with the current state". The HTTP layer maps them for you.
options:
401 Log in first
403 Missing permission
409 Not enough stock

403 Log in first
401 Missing permission
409 Not enough stock

401 Log in first
403 Missing permission
400 Not enough stock

500 Log in first
500 Missing permission
500 Not enough stock

questions.q: What does the checkout schema say about these three bodies?
questions.explain: An empty cart and a negative quantity are both refused before the database is touched (400). Limits on the array and the quantity also stop a single request from asking for millions of items.
options: [ false, false, true ]
[ true, false, true ]
[ false, true, true ]
[ true, true, true ]

questions.q: Why does /login have its own rate limiter?
questions.explain: Password hashing is slow on purpose, and login is the favourite target of guessing attacks. Milestone 1 adds a second limit per e-mail.
options: To reduce the server's electricity bill
To stop password guessing: after 5 attempts a minute from one address, login answers 429
Because /login is the slowest route
So each user can only log in once a day

questions.q: The "never oversells" test fires four checkouts at the same time for a product with two left. What must it require?
questions.explain: With Promise.allSettled, count the fulfilled results. Remove AND stock >= $1 on purpose and watch the test fail: that is how you know it protects something.
options: All four succeed
Exactly two succeed and the stock ends at 0
Exactly one succeeds
All four fail with 409

questions.q: Why should the "never oversells" test also run against a real PostgreSQL server in CI?
questions.explain: A race needs things to really happen at the same time. PGlite is great for fast, isolated tests, but it is gentler than production.
options: PGlite does not support UPDATE
PGlite runs one transaction at a time, so it can hide a race that appears with several real connections
Real PostgreSQL is faster for tests
Vitest cannot run PGlite

questions.q: Milestone 3: GET /orders/:id for someone else's order. What should it answer, and how?
questions.explain: Putting the owner in the SQL means an order that is not yours is never even loaded, so one forgotten check cannot leak data. 404 instead of 403 means nobody can learn which order ids exist.
options: 403, after loading the order and comparing owners
404, with the owner in the SQL: WHERE id = $1 AND user_id = $2
200, because order ids are not secret
401, and log the user out

questions.q: This finds an order the way the lesson's one(userId, orderId) does. What does it print?
questions.explain: Order 2 exists but belongs to user 3, and order 3 does not exist at all. Both answer the same 404, so user 2 cannot tell which ids are real.
options:
200 2400
404 No order 2
404 No order 3

200 2400
403 No order 2
404 No order 3

200 2400
404 No order 2
403 No order 3

questions.q: The milestones say "parameterized SQL only". Which query follows that rule?
questions.explain: With $1 the value travels separately from the SQL text, so it can never change the query. Building SQL with strings, even after a conversion, is the habit that leads to injection.
options: db.query(`SELECT * FROM orders WHERE user_id = ${userId}`)
db.query("SELECT * FROM orders WHERE user_id = '" + userId + "'")
db.query("SELECT id FROM orders WHERE user_id = $1", [userId])
db.query("SELECT * FROM orders WHERE user_id = " + Number(userId))

questions.q: Milestone 4 adds a support role. Which permission list fits "may read every order and cancel one, but may not touch products or roles"?
questions.explain: Give each role only what it needs (least privilege). A wildcard such as *:* or product:* would let support staff change prices or roles.
options: ["*:*"]
["order:read", "order:cancel"]
["order:*", "product:*"]
["role:update", "order:read"]

questions.q: Finish takeStock(products, sku, quantity) like the conditional UPDATE: if the product exists and has at least quantity in stock, reduce it and return { priceCents }; otherwise change nothing and return null. The program should print 1200 null null and then stock: 0.
questions.explain: Check and change together, with nothing in between, and return the price from the stored product. An empty result is the "not enough stock" signal, like an empty RETURNING.

questions.q: Finish orderTotal(items, catalog). Each item has sku, quantity and maybe a priceCents sent by the client. Use only the catalog's price, never the client's. The program should print 4400.
questions.explain: 2 × 1200 + 1 × 2000 = 4400 cents. The client's priceCents: 1 is ignored: a client must never be able to choose its own price.

questions.q: Finish checkout(stock, items) so it is all or nothing: work on a copy of stock; for each item, throw new Error(`Not enough stock for ${sku}`) if there is not enough, otherwise take it. Only when every item worked, copy the new values back into stock. The program should print Not enough stock for mug and then { tee: 5, mug: 0 }.
questions.explain: The T-shirt line worked on the copy, but the mug failed, so the copy is thrown away and the real stock still shows 5 T-shirts. A database transaction gives you exactly this, with ROLLBACK.
questions.expected:
Not enough stock for mug
{ tee: 5, mug: 0 }

questions.q: Finish registrationData(body). Return only { email, password, role }, where email is trimmed and lower-cased, and role is always "customer", whatever the body says. The program should print { email: 'ada@example.com', password: 's3cret-pass', role: 'customer' }.
questions.explain: Pick the fields you want instead of copying the whole body. Anything the client adds, such as role or isAdmin, simply never reaches the database.

questions.q: Finish getOrder(orders, userId, orderId). Return { status: 200, body: order } when the order exists and belongs to userId, otherwise { status: 404, body: { error: "Not found" } }, also when it belongs to someone else. The program should print 200 404 404.
questions.explain: Search by id and owner in one condition, like WHERE id = $1 AND user_id = $2. Someone else's order and a missing order look the same, so ids cannot be probed.

questions.q: Finish bearer(header). Return the token after "Bearer ", or undefined when the header is missing or does not start with "Bearer ". The program should print abc123 undefined undefined.
questions.explain: The identity comes only from this token, which the server hashes and looks up. ?. handles a missing header, and "Bearer ".length is 7.

questions.q: Finish authorize(user, permission) with the permission engine. Build an actor from String(user.id) with roles: [user.role], and throw new AuthorizationError(`Missing permission ${permission}`) when can returns false. The program should print ok and then 403 Missing permission product:create.
questions.explain: The role comes from the user loaded from the database, never from the request. can is async, so await it before you check the result.

questions.q: Finish checkout(id, inStock). Call transaction(work), where work throws new Error("Not enough stock") when inStock is false. Publish order.placed with { orderId: id } on the bus only after the transaction succeeded, and return "201"; on an error return "409". The program should print 201 409 and receipts: [ 1 ].
questions.explain: Publish after the transaction returns, never inside it. The failed order 2 gets no receipt, because no listener ever hears about a rolled-back order.

questions.q: Finish formatCents(cents) so it shows whole cents as money with two decimals and a dollar sign. The program should print $24.00 $0.05 $1234.50.
questions.explain: Store and add whole cents; divide by 100 only for display. toFixed(2) always shows two decimals.

questions.explain: The same token always gives the same hash, so the server can look it up. Someone who steals the hash from the database cannot log in with it: the server would hash it again and find nothing.

questions.q: Login allows 5 attempts per minute from one address. What does this print?
questions.explain: The first five wrong passwords get 401. The sixth attempt in the window gets 429 Too Many Requests, so a password cannot be guessed by trying thousands of them.

questions.q: The order.placed listener clears the product cache. What does this print?
questions.explain: Until the event is published, the cache still holds the old stock. The listener clears the entry, so the next read loads the new stock. Checkout itself does not know about the cache.
options:
mug: 2 left
mug: 0 left

mug: 0 left
mug: 0 left

mug: 2 left
mug: 2 left

undefined
